# He et al., Cursor adoption, development velocity and code quality in open-source projects

**Source:** Hao He, Courtney Miller, Shyam Agarwal, Christian Kästner and Bogdan Vasilescu (Carnegie Mellon University), "Speed at the Cost of Quality: How Cursor AI Increases Short-Term Velocity and Long-Term Complexity in Open-Source Projects", arXiv:2511.04427v3, 26 Jan 2026; MSR '26 (ACM), DOI 10.1145/3793302.3793349. CC BY 4.0. Scope: open.
**Structure:** A 19-page empirical paper: introduction and related work; a staggered difference-in-differences design with propensity-matched controls and dynamic panel GMM models; stated threats to validity; results on velocity, quality and their interaction, with robustness checks; discussion, practical implications and conclusion; appendices on matching, alternative estimators, further robustness checks and the types of new static analysis warnings.

## Author's Thesis (condensed)

The authors estimate the causal effect of adopting Cursor, an LLM agent assistant, on development velocity and software quality in open-source GitHub projects, because practitioners report multifold productivity gains without empirical evidence, and because findings on completion and chat tools cannot be extrapolated to agentic tools (Abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 1). They find a statistically significant, large but transient rise in project-level velocity alongside a substantial, persistent rise in static analysis warnings and code complexity; panel GMM models indicate that the accumulated warnings and complexity then slow future velocity, a self-reinforcing cycle (Abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 2). Cursor adoption still raises complexity when the models control for velocity dynamics (§1, p. 2).

They conclude that quality assurance is a major bottleneck for early adopters, that sustained benefits need process adaptations which scale quality assurance with AI-era velocity, and that tools should treat quality as a first-class design concern (Abstract, p. 1; §1, p. 2). They present the evidence as challenging both unbridled optimism and categorical pessimism (§6, p. 11). The estimates are intent-to-treat effects of visible adoption in open-source repositories with at least 10 stars, observed January 2024 to August 2025, measured against a state of practice that may already include other AI tools (§3.1.2, p. 4; §3.2, p. 5; §3.5.1, p. 7).

## The Question and the Prior Evidence

Agentic assistants like Cursor work inside the IDE with persistent codebase awareness, navigating files and implementing features across dozens of files, where completion and chat tools leave the developer as primary agent overseeing AI-generated code at a granular level (§1, p. 1). The authors list the consequences: automation shifts from typing to whole workflows; integration may bring both gains and over-reliance or less rigorous review; reviewing large multi-file AI changes differs from reviewing completions; and technical debt may build over time (§1, pp. 1–2). Becker et al. found early-2025 tools, Cursor included, did not speed up experienced open-source developers on real tasks, and Watanabe et al. found 83.8% of 567 Claude Code pull requests accepted, but Watanabe et al. analysed acceptance rates and task types, not project-level effects over months (§1, p. 2).

Prior Copilot-era studies report productivity gains of 21% to 56% in small randomized experiments and 22% to 36% in field experiments, with similar or lower observational estimates from open source (17.82% more Python releases; 6.5% more accepted pull requests; 2.4% more quarterly commits at 30% AI use) (§2, p. 3). Quality studies report that LLMs may generate code with security, performance, smell and outdated-API problems, with inconclusive evidence on complexity; the authors know of no prior study that systematically investigated project-level quality outcomes in the wild after LLM adoption (§2, p. 3). Gray-literature claims of multifold gains run orders of magnitude above any empirical estimate for earlier tools (§2, p. 3).

## Research Design

The first commit touching `.cursorrules` files or `.cursor` folders serves as a proxy for the adoption date; this captures a mix of Cursor's Composer multi-file editing (mid-2024) and its agent mode (released November 2024, default February 2025) (§1, p. 2 and fn. 1). From 23,308 Cursor files in 3,306 non-fork repositories, a 10-star threshold left 806 adopting repositories, most adopting between August 2024 and March 2025; the median adopter had 3 contributors and 51 stars (§1, p. 2; §3.1.2, p. 4; Table 1, p. 4). Controls are three nearest neighbours per adopter, same primary language, chosen by propensity models built from six months of GHArchive activity trajectory plus earlier history (AUC 0.83 to 0.91), giving 1,380 never-adopters (§1, p. 2; §3.1.3, pp. 4–5). The authors report the matching as imperfect: covariates are in acceptable balance but mean differences remain, and the models explain only 14% to 27% of adoption variance (Appendix A, p. 14).

Monthly outcomes are commits and lines added for velocity, and three SonarQube maintainability metrics for quality: static analysis warnings (read as an estimate of the effort to review potential issues), duplicate line density, and cognitive code complexity (§3.2.1, p. 5). The Borusyak et al. imputation estimator gives average and month-by-month (horizon) effects, avoiding the bias two-way fixed effects can show under staggered adoption; all outcomes pass pre-trend tests (§3.3.3, p. 6; §4.1, pp. 7–8). Arellano-Bond dynamic panel GMM models test four paths between lines added, warnings and complexity, with a Cursor-adoption dummy (§3.4, p. 6).

## Threats to Validity the Authors State

The authors ask readers to interpret the results in the context of the setup and its limits (§3.5.1, p. 7). Only committed configuration files reveal adoption, so the sample is visible adopters, which could make the estimates an upper bound or conservative; the authors see it as repositories where adoption is deliberate, visible practice change (§3.5.1, p. 7). A configuration file shows only that someone experimented, and continued use is assumed unless removal is observed, so the estimates are intent-to-treat effects (§3.5.1, p. 7). Cursor version and model backend are unknown; unobserved confounders such as expertise, team practices and culture may remain after matching; and other AI tools may be in use on both sides, so the comparison is with the state of practice, not with no AI (§3.5.1, p. 7).

Results may not generalize to other agents, proprietary software or languages beyond JavaScript, TypeScript and Python, and may not persist as tools and workflows mature (§3.5.2, p. 7). The quality findings depend on the estimator and should be read with caution (Appendix B.3, p. 16). Composer and agent users cannot be clearly separated (Appendix C, p. 17); complexity metrics were designed for human-written code (§6, p. 11); and the warning-category analysis rests on a convenience sample (Appendix D, p. 18).

## Velocity and Quality Results

Lines added rise by about 28.6% on average (p < 0.05), with no significant effect on commits (§4.1.1, p. 8; Table 2, p. 7). The only significant velocity gain is in the first two months: commits up 55.4% then 14.5%, lines added up 281.3% then 48.4%, described in the introduction as 3-5x in the first month (§4.1.1, p. 8; §1, p. 2). Static analysis warnings rise by 30.3% and code complexity by 41.6% on average, and both rises persist beyond the adoption period; duplicate line density shows no significant change (§4.1.2, p. 8).

In the GMM models, holding other dynamics constant, velocity has no significant effect on warnings or complexity, and growth in codebase size absorbs most of their variance; Cursor adoption has no significant effect on warnings, but still raises complexity by a 9% baseline on average among projects in similar dynamics (§4.2, p. 8). By the GMM estimates, a 100% rise in complexity or warnings causes a 64.5% or 50.3% fall in lines added, and adoption brings a 1.84x baseline rise in lines added, so the velocity gain would be cancelled by a ∼5x rise in warnings or a ∼3x rise in complexity (§4.2, p. 8).

## Robustness Checks

Where contributors who touched Cursor files made at least 80% of commits, or in months with Cursor-file edits, the quality effects are stronger, which the authors read as strengthening the causal reading; velocity still rises in months with Cursor-file edits, suggesting that abandonment cancels part of the gains (§4.3, p. 9). Findings persist, weaker, in very active repositories (at least 10 commits a month) (§4.3, p. 9). Of the treatment repositories, 382 may use other AI tools; contamination weakens the estimates, and the findings are stronger where other tools are less likely (§4.3, p. 10). Results are qualitatively consistent across JavaScript/TypeScript, Python and Go, and across cohorts before and after agent release, though the cohort split shows slightly weaker estimated effects on warnings and complexity (Appendix C, pp. 16–17).

Under alternative estimators, the velocity horizon estimates agree qualitatively; for quality, two-way fixed effects also finds significant rises in warnings and complexity, but the Callaway and Sant'Anna estimator gives negative, non-significant estimates, which the authors say may stem from small cohorts with noisy quality metrics, or from differing covariate adjustment (Appendix B.3, pp. 15–16). In a descriptive sample of 195,010 warnings, 16 of 20 categories rose after adoption, led by naming conventions, leftover artefacts (code hygiene), complexity and style, with smaller rises in logic errors and security; API usage and concurrency warnings fell (Appendix D, p. 18).

## The Authors' Interpretation

The velocity-quality dynamic alone likely does not fully explain why the gain vanishes after two months, since cancellation would need an unlikely rise in complexity or warnings (§5.1.1, p. 10). Another explanation, which they call highly plausible, is an excitement-frustration-abandonment cycle: novelty and use on tasks where AI excels, then frustration where AI is limited (intricate debugging, understanding existing code, edge cases), plus the overhead of verifying and debugging AI output, which may lead to reduced use or abandonment (§5.1.1, p. 10).

On quality, much of the warning rise follows from faster code production growing the codebase; agent assistants amplify existing velocity-quality dynamics and may not add more issues than non-adopters moving at the same speed, so quality assurance needs to scale with AI-era velocity (§5.1.2, p. 10). Complexity is different: its rise after accounting for velocity is, for the authors, strong evidence that Cursor-generated code in their sample is inherently more complex than human-written code, a "complexity debt" in projects that use AI heavily, which may raise frustration and maintenance costs later (§5.1.2, p. 10). They tie the findings to open-source conditions (easy abandonment, distributed collaboration, intrinsic motivation, scarce QA resources) and suggest that in enterprises mandates, sunk training costs and oversight might sustain use and lead to distinct temporal patterns, while mandatory review, automated testing and dedicated QA might prevent proportional debt accumulation (§5.1.3, pp. 10–11).

## Practical Implications

To get past what they call the technical debt accumulation ratchet, the authors suggest refactoring sprints triggered by quality metrics, test coverage requirements that scale with lines added, and engineered Cursor rules that enforce quality standards; without such changes, the initial surge may push a project toward an unmaintainable end state (§5.2, p. 11). The authors describe the agents of the study period as generation-first and want tools that suggest tests, flag unnecessary complexity in real time, recommend refactoring and might throttle their own output when project complexity or debt passes healthy thresholds (§5.2, p. 11). They call the complexity rise a "comprehension tax" and suggest teams give AI-generated code extra scrutiny in review, asking whether a simpler implementation would do (§5.2, p. 11). The conclusion offers three reasons for less pessimism: the study is a mid-2024 to mid-2025 snapshot, the quality metrics may miss aspects of quality, and the open-source context may amplify the effects (§6, p. 11).

## Key Statistics

- Sample: 806 adopting repositories (Table 7's main setting: 801 treatment, 1,172 control), 1,380 matched never-adopters reported in §1; median 3 contributors and 51 stars (§1, p. 2; §3.1.2, p. 4; Tables 1 and 7).
- Average effects (Borusyak): lines added +28.58% (p < 0.05); commits +2.63% (n.s.); warnings +30.26% and complexity +41.64% (p < 0.001); duplicate density +7.03% (n.s.) (Table 2, p. 7).
- First and second month: commits +55.4% and +14.5%; lines added +281.3% and +48.4% (§4.1.1, p. 8).
- GMM: Cursor → complexity, 9% baseline increase; Cursor → lines added, 1.84x baseline increase; 100% rise in complexity or warnings → 64.5% or 50.3% fall in lines added; cancellation at ∼5x warnings or ∼3x complexity (§4.2, p. 8).
- Alternative estimators for lines added: +82.74% (TWFE), +53.60% (Callaway and Sant'Anna); Callaway and Sant'Anna warnings −10.49% and complexity −3.80%, both n.s. (Table 6, p. 16).
- Other AI tools: 382 treatment repositories may use them (§4.3, p. 10).
- Warning sample: 195,010 warnings, 933 rules; 16 of 20 categories up; change in mean new warnings per repository per month, pre- to post-adoption: logic errors +2.09, security +1.98 (Appendix D, Table 8, p. 18).
- Note: the paper also gives the complexity increase as 25.1% (§5.1.2) and 25% (§5.2), against 41.64% in Table 2.

## Key Connections

- Becker et al.: early-2025 AI tools, Cursor included, did not speed up experienced open-source developers (§1, p. 2; §2, p. 3).
- Watanabe et al.: 83.8% of 567 Claude Code pull requests accepted (§1, p. 2).
- Earlier Copilot productivity studies (Peng et al., Song et al., Cui et al., Pandey et al., Yeverechyahu et al., Daniotti et al.): the prior range of estimates (§2, p. 3).
- Borusyak, Jaravel and Spiess; Callaway and Sant'Anna; two-way fixed effects critiques (Goodman-Bacon; De Chaisemartin and d'Haultfoeuille; Athey and Imbens): the estimators (§3.3.3, p. 6; Appendix B).
- Arellano and Bond: dynamic panel GMM (§3.4, p. 6).
- Campbell and SonarQube: cognitive complexity (§3.2.1, p. 5).
- Besker et al. and Cheng et al.: technical debt reducing productivity (§3.4, p. 6; §5.1.1, p. 10).
- Kumar et al.: an enterprise study indicating different temporal patterns of AI tool use (§5.1.3, p. 11).
- GitClear's Copilot data: an example of the simplistic narrative the authors challenge (§5.1.2, p. 10).
- Pluralistic: all code is a liability (§5.1.2, p. 10).

## Signature Contrarian Positions

1. Against unbridled optimism about AI-assisted coding: empirical evidence is lacking around self-reported multifold productivity claims, which run orders of magnitude above any empirical estimate for earlier tools (Abstract, p. 1; §2, p. 3; §6, p. 11).
2. Findings on completion and chat tools cannot be extrapolated to agentic assistants (§1, p. 1).
3. Against simplistic narratives that AI coding degrades quality: much of the warning rise follows velocity and codebase growth, and the evidence challenges categorical pessimism too (§5.1.2, p. 10; §6, p. 11).
4. Two-way fixed effects can bias estimates under staggered adoption (§3.3.3, p. 6; Appendix B.1, p. 15).
5. Generation-first tool design leaves quality maintenance as an afterthought (§5.2, p. 11).
